reviews.reasoning: The closing seam is well made and I do not contest it: 71:9 opens with the negative petition אַֽל תַּ֭שְׁלִיכֵנִי and carries זִקְנָ֑ה, so “Don’t reject me in my old age.” (web:Ps.71.9) is a genuine mood and vocabulary shift away from the retrospective, and the spelling זקנה occurs in 2 of the psalm's 24 verses (9 and 18). The Psalm 22 arithmetic is right and I re-derived it through ps_lib: Ps 22 is shift+1, so web:Ps.22.9 = oshb:Ps.22.10 and web:Ps.22.10 = oshb:Ps.22.11, exactly as the refs array has it, and the cluster's WEB quotations re-check clean (check_web_quotes: 37 quotes, 0 flags). The row hedges its Psalm 22 link as texture rather than a driver, correctly, so I do not fault it for arguing that parallel in English -- though sharper evidence sat in the bytes, where 71:6 עָלֶ֤יךָ נִסְמַ֬כְתִּי מִבֶּ֗טֶן and 22:11 עָ֭לֶיךָ הָשְׁלַ֣כְתִּי מֵרָ֑חֶם share a fronted עליך plus מבטן pattern. What I contest is the opening warrant, which rests on a particle this psalm itself shows to be seam-neutral.

challenges.claim: The row's stated opening signal -- a verse-initial causal particle at 71:5 -- cannot carry the 71:4|71:5 seam, because the same verse-initial particle at 71:10 introduces a ground clause that continues its strophe rather than opening one.
challenges.evidence: Verse-initial splices: 71:5 begins כִּֽי and 71:10 begins כִּֽי; each collates at byte tier against its own verse and the 2 splices are byte-identical to each other (oshb:Ps.71.5, oshb:Ps.71.10; identity psalm). Both witnesses read them alike -- “For you are my hope, Lord Yahweh, my confidence from my youth.” (web:Ps.71.5) and “For my enemies talk about me.” (web:Ps.71.10). The 2 occurrences stand in parallel structural positions: petition at 71:1-4 followed by its ground at 71:5, petition at 71:9 followed by its ground at 71:10 -- and the second pair is treated, rightly, as strophe-internal continuation by the row spanning 71:9-71:13. A subordinating causal particle links backward to what it grounds, so at 71:5 it is evidence for cohesion with the preceding petitions, not for a seam before them. The row's observed_substrate_signals field holds 2 entries, this particle and a register description, so the seam is left with 0 signals that discriminate 71:5 from 71:10. Compounding it, the refuge bracket 71:1 חָסִ֑יתִי / 71:7 מַֽחֲסִי (2 of 24 verses by skeleton sweep of חסי) crosses this row's opening seam undisclosed. The seam may survive on a re-warranted basis, but the replacement warrant has to pass the test that kills this one -- it must distinguish 71:5 from 71:10.

reviews.reasoning: The span holds together and its 2 outer seams are sound: 71:9 opens the old-age petition, and 71:14 opens וַ֭אֲנִי (oshb:Ps.71.14, byte tier), a fronted pronoun the next row rightly reads as the adversative pivot. The quoted-speech frame the row leans on is byte-real -- 71:11 opens לֵ֭אמֹר, introducing the taunt “God has forsaken him.” (web:Ps.71.11) -- and the cluster's WEB quotations re-check clean (check_web_quotes: 37 quotes, 0 flags). challenges.claim: The rejected_alternative rejects a break after 71:11 on the ground that what follows continues 'without a new vocative or topic shift', but 71:12 opens with a vocative, carries a second one, and turns from third-person report about the enemies to direct address to God -- an addressee shift landing precisely at the rival seam.
challenges.evidence: Verse-initial splice: 71:12 begins אֱ֭לֹהִים and carries אֱ֝לֹהַ֗י as its fifth of 8 words (oshb:Ps.71.12, byte tier). WEB agrees: “God, don’t be far from me. My God, hurry to help me.” (web:Ps.71.12). The contrast with what precedes is byte-visible rather than interpretive -- a skeleton sweep of אלהי over Psalm 71 returns 7 of the psalm's 24 verses (4, 11, 12, 17, 18, 19, 22) and 71:10 is not among them, so the report opens with 1 verse carrying no divine name at all, while the אֱלֹהִ֣ים standing in 71:11 is the third-person SUBJECT of the enemies' quoted speech, “God has forsaken him.” (web:Ps.71.11), not an address by the psalmist. The seam at 71:11|71:12 is therefore where divine address returns after a 2-verse stretch of report about the enemies: a tier-1 speech-frame and addressee shift, and the tier-1 signal the rival had. The row's own rationale concedes the substance in other words, calling 71:12 'an imperative counter-petition' addressed to God, so rationale and rejected_alternative contradict each other. The rival may still be rightly rejected -- the conspiracy topic does run on through 71:13, where מְ֝בַקְשֵׁ֗י רָעָתִֽי closes the imprecation -- but not on the ground given, and a replacement ground must survive the vocative at 71:12.

challenges.claim: The row's closing-seam warrant -- that 71:19 opens with a rhetorical 'who is like you' exclamation -- misdescribes verse-final material as verse-initial in both witnesses, and it is stated 2 times, in the rationale and again in the rejected_alternative.
challenges.evidence: MT 71:19 opens וְצִדְקָתְךָ֥ and closes מִ֣י כָמֽוֹךָ -- the exclamation is the verse's last 2 of 10 words (oshb:Ps.71.19, byte tier; a skeleton sweep of מי כמוך over Psalm 71 returns 1 verse, 71:19, at that final position). WEB puts it in the same place: the verse opens “God, your righteousness also reaches to the heavens.” and its third and last sentence is “God, who is like you?” (web:Ps.71.19). The actual verse-initial element is a waw-conjunctive noun phrase continuing 71:18's declaration of divine attributes -- 71:18 תַּעַ֫זְבֵ֥נִי into 71:19 וְצִדְקָתְךָ֥ -- which WEB marks with 'also', while 71:18 ends “your might to everyone who is to come.” (web:Ps.71.18). The righteousness spelling צדקת occurs in 5 of the psalm's 24 verses (2, 15, 16, 19, 24), 2 of them inside this row's own span, so the lexeme opening 71:19 is a thread running through the row rather than a fresh address. The seam may be defensible on other grounds, but as written the warrant asserts a text-fact the bytes contradict, on a row carrying 'high' confidence -- a calibration failure as well as an evidence one. A replacement warrant must pass the test that killed this one, and the driver swap re-opens observed_substrate_signals, rejected_alternative and confidence together.

challenges.evidence: Same bytes as the seam partner: MT 71:19 opens וְצִדְקָתְךָ֥ and closes מִ֣י כָמֽוֹךָ (oshb:Ps.71.19, byte tier); in WEB the verse opens “God, your righteousness also reaches to the heavens.” with “God, who is like you?” as its third and last sentence (web:Ps.71.19). The declarative opening clauses are וְצִדְקָתְךָ֥ אֱלֹהִ֗ים עַד מָ֫ר֥וֹם and אֲשֶׁר עָשִׂ֥יתָ גְדֹל֑וֹת; 2 of the verse's 10 words are interrogative, so 'a rhetorical exclamation' describes a fifth of the verse. 'A fresh address' also runs against the waw-conjunctive opener, which WEB renders 'also', and against the righteousness spelling צדקת appearing in 5 of the psalm's 24 verses (2, 15, 16, 19, 24). This is the seam-pair image of the defect on the 71:14-71:18 row: one cure, authored once and installed on both rows in the same pass.

challenges.claim: The row quotes 71:20 twice from WEB as its restoration plea without disclosing that the verse carries 2 of the book's 68 ketiv/qere notes, both of them the 1cp/1cs person alternation, and that the plural of the clause it quotes is not the person the pointed MT text carries at that word.
challenges.evidence: pmarks_Ps.json records 2 K/Q notes at Ps.71.20 (single-witness WLC), and the bytes show both pairs as unpointed ketiv beside pointed qere: הראיתנו against הִרְאִיתַ֨נִי, and תחיינו against תְּחַיֵּ֑ינִי (oshb:Ps.71.20). Both pairs are the same alternation -- 1st person plural in the ketiv, 1st person singular in the qere -- and WEB visibly splits between them inside the 1 verse, rendering “who have shown us many and bitter troubles” on one side and “you will let me live” on the other (web:Ps.71.20). The third verb has no ketiv twin among the verse's 13 tokens: the MT reads תַּעֲלֵֽנִי, 1st person singular, while the clause the row quotes as the span's restoration plea is “You will bring us up again from the depths of the earth.” (web:Ps.71.20), a plural the pointed text does not carry at that word. The row then builds a person contrast on it, setting that plea against “Increase my honor and comfort me again.” (web:Ps.71.21) in its closing signal, so the argument leans on an English person that is a rendering divergence at 1 word and a ketiv/qere selection at 2 others. This is a disclosure defect, not a reading selection: the variant zone is held, and the cure is to disclose the K/Q and the person divergence where the verse is quoted.

reviews.reasoning: Re-derivation of this row's claims turned up 0 false statements. The 71:21|71:22 seam is real: 71:22 opens גַּם אֲנִ֤י (oshb:Ps.71.22, byte tier) and the instruments sit in its opening clause -- the spellings נבל and כנור each occur in 1 of the psalm's 24 verses, both at 71:22 -- so “I will also praise you with the harp for your faithfulness, my God.” (web:Ps.71.22) does open a distinct movement against the imperative “Increase my honor and comfort me again.” (web:Ps.71.21). The 71:13-to-71:24 return the row claims is byte-checkable and true: the shame root shows at 71:13 יֵבֹ֣שׁוּ and 71:24 בֹ֥שׁוּ, and the accusers' phrase is skeleton-identical at both, מְ֝בַקְשֵׁ֗י רָעָתִֽי and מְבַקְשֵׁ֥י רָעָתִֽי (2 of 24 verses by skeleton sweep of מבקשי רעתי). WEB quotations are verbatim and no dual-cite is owed in an identity psalm. Three observations that I judged do NOT rise to defects, since nothing the row states is false. (a) The cited pairing is the weaker half of what the bytes offer: of the row's 'disappointed...confounded' pair only the first recurs at 71:13, the second resting on חָ֝פְר֗וּ, whose spelling חפר occurs in 1 of the psalm's 24 verses; the element that actually repeats across the 2 verses is the accusers' phrase, which the row quotes in English but does not identify as the repeated item. (b) The row's 'closing inclusio' would anchor better at the psalm's opening: the shame root brackets 71:1 אֵב֥וֹשָׁה against 71:24 בֹ֥שׁוּ, a sweep of 3 verses across 2 spellings (plene בוש at 1 verse, 71:1; defective בש at 2 verses, 71:13 and 71:24), and all 3 render alike in WEB -- “Never let me be disappointed.” (web:Ps.71.1), “Let my accusers be disappointed and consumed.” (web:Ps.71.13), “for they are disappointed, and they are confounded, who want to harm me.” (web:Ps.71.24). (c) The verse-initial pivot at the row's own seam is גַּם אֲנִ֤י, standing in a fronted-pronoun series with וַ֭אֲנִי at 71:14 and גַּם לְשׁוֹנִ֗י at 71:24; the row warrants the seam on instrument vocabulary instead, which is defensible but leaves the stronger tier-1 opener unused.
